title: India's Supreme Court Declares Right to Walk on Footpaths a Fundamental Right
excerpt: The landmark ruling places pedestrian safety above motorised vehicle movement and directs the Centre to create a statutory framework protecting walkers.
body:
• The Supreme Court declared the right to walk on demarcated footpaths a fundamental right under Articles 19(1)(d) and 21 of the Constitution, with priority over motorised vehicles.
  • Urban development authorities, municipal corporations, and panchayats now have an enforceable duty to build, maintain, and keep footpaths free from encroachments.
  • The court directed the Centre to consider enacting a dedicated pedestrian rights law and establishing a regulatory body to enforce it.

India's Supreme Court has declared that the right to walk on safe, demarcated footpaths is a fundamental right under the Constitution — one that takes precedence over the movement of motorised vehicles on public roads.

The June 19 judgment by Justices P.S. Narasimha and Atul S. Chandurkar came in a motor accident claim arising from the death of a five-year-old boy who was killed by a tanker while walking to school with his father. There was neither a footpath nor a pedestrian crossing on the stretch of road where the accident occurred.

A Constitutional Foundation for Pedestrians

Justice Narasimha, who authored the judgment, grounded the right to walk in Article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution — the right to move freely throughout India — read alongside Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b), 19(1)(c), and Article 21, the right to life and personal liberty.

https://x.com/AndhraNexus/status/2084220383713231092

"The fundamental right to walk will take within its sweep the right to demarcated footpaths. These rights are primary and shall have priority over movement by motorised vehicles."

— Justice P.S. Narasimha, Supreme Court of India

The court observed that walking is the "simplest of the simple human activity, inextricably connected to life" and noted that rapid urbanisation and the dominance of motorised transport had pushed pedestrians to the margins. "Wheels eclipsed our imagination, and our municipal authorities were busy creating roads that were suitable for motorized people," Justice Narasimha wrote.

Enforceable Duty on Authorities

The ruling places a direct, enforceable duty on urban development authorities, municipal corporations, municipalities, and panchayats to demarcate, construct, maintain, and safeguard footpaths and pedestrian infrastructure on every road.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=HrnAjOGkZ4U

"If a road exists, there must then be a duty to ensure that a footpath is demarcated and maintained for the walkers. This is an enforceable duty," the bench held, according to The Hindu Business Line.

Violations of this right would entitle citizens to invoke constitutional and legal remedies — including compensation and restitution — against the responsible authorities. These remedies are independent of those available under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, which the court said "has been an impediment and, in many ways, undermined the precious rights of walkers."

Centre Told to Legislate

The bench directed its Registry to send the judgment to the Ministries of Housing and Urban Affairs, Rural Development, and Road Transport and Highways, urging them to "reflect on the compelling necessity for initiating the necessary legal framework." A copy was also sent to the Law Commission of India to examine a statutory framework for protecting pedestrian rights.

The court called for a dedicated regulatory body with domain expertise to plan, enforce, and implement the right to walk. The case has been re-numbered as a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, titled "Re: Fundamental Right to Walk and Footpath," with the Government of India impleaded — keeping the issue alive for further hearings, according to Mondaq.

Diaspora Resonance

For members of the Indian diaspora, the ruling strikes a chord. Anyone who has navigated the chaotic, often footpath-less streets of Indian cities — from Delhi to Chennai — recognises the daily danger pedestrians face. The contrast with pedestrian infrastructure in cities like New York, London, or Sydney is stark. The judgment opens a legal pathway for NRIs and returning residents to hold local authorities accountable for unsafe walking conditions near family homes, schools, and temples.

What's Next

The immediate impact is the enhanced compensation of ₹11,44,628 awarded to the father of the five-year-old victim, to be paid within two months. But the broader implications will unfold over months as the Centre decides whether to introduce a pedestrian rights law in Parliament.

The court's direction to establish a full-time regulator — if acted upon — could transform how Indian cities plan roads and public spaces. Whether municipal bodies across the country comply with the ruling, and how quickly encroachments on existing footpaths are cleared, will be the real test of this landmark declaration.
